p: VanderKam's text names the boy Serug at once; the text Charles used calls him Seroh and renames him in 11:6.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
readings.en: and he called his name Serug

readings.w: Charles's translation (1902; 1913), made from his own Ge'ez text
readings.en: and he called his name Seroh

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's text, the base text of this site. In Charles's text the play on the name in 11:6 is a renaming (Seroh becomes Serug); in VanderKam's it explains the name the boy already has.
b: Charles 1902 notes a suggestion that Seroh comes from a Hebrew verb for sinning, but argues that 11:6 explains the name from sur, "turn aside."

a: In the seventh year of the sixth week
p: VanderKam's text gives no number for the year; the text Charles translated has 'the seventh year.'

readings.w: Charles's translation (1902; 1913), made from his own Ge'ez text
readings.en: in the sixth week, in the seventh year of it
readings.plain: In the seventh year of the sixth week

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); the EOTC printed Bible (digital copy) reads the same, with the usual spelling of the word for week
readings.orig: ወኮነ በኡባዔ ሳድስ ዓመቱ ሎቱ (wäkonä bäʾubaʿe sads ʿamätu lotu)
readings.en: and it was in the sixth week, its year
readings.plain: In a year of the sixth week

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from VanderKam's text. As printed, the Ge'ez says only "in the sixth week, its year," which looks like a number has dropped out. The text Charles translated has "seventh," and the Plain English Translation follows it. The EOTC copy is not an independent witness: it agrees with VanderKam word for word here except that VanderKam's printed text spells the word for "week" ʾubaʿe, a slip for subaʿe.

p: The Ge'ez says Abram came into Asshur (Assyria). One of Charles's manuscripts has Sur; Charles suspected 'Canaan.'

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
readings.en: and he came into Asur

readings.w: Charles's manuscript a, as cited in Charles 1902
readings.en: and he came into Sur

readings.w: Charles's suggested correction (1902), not found in any manuscript
readings.en: and he came into Canaan

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the base text. Asshur makes poor geography for a road from Haran to Shechem, and Charles marked it as corrupt, but no manuscript he knew reads "Canaan." The verse has already said that Abram set out for the land of Canaan.

p: The Latin has Bahalot, the town Bealoth; the Ge'ez has a garbled form that reads like 'until Lot came.'

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.en: to Bealoth

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
readings.en: as far as Boa Lot (or: until Lot came)

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from VanderKam's text and follows the Latin. Charles 1902 judged the Ge'ez form corrupt and saw, following Littmann, that the Latin Bahalot is Bealoth, a town in the far south of Judah (Joshua 15:24), which fits "the land of the south." The Ge'ez letters can be read as "until Lot entered," which makes no sense here.

a: Abram went and killed Chedorlaomer and came back. He set aside a tenth of everything and gave it to Melchizedek. This tithe
t: The gap where Melchizedek should be
p: In VanderKam's text these words stand in square brackets. The manuscripts Charles used have a gap here.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989), the words printed in square brackets
readings.orig: ወሖረ አብራም ወቀተሎ ለከደለጎሞር ወየመይጠ ወዐሠረ ዐሥራተ እምኵሉ ወወሀቦ ለመልከ ጼዴቅ ወዝንቱ ዐሥራት (wäḥorä ʾäbram wäqätälo läkädälägomor wäyämäyṭä wäʿäśärä ʿäśratä ʾəmkʷəlu wäwähäbo lämälkä ṣedeq wäznətu ʿäśrat)
readings.en: and Abram went and killed Chedorlaomer and returned, and tithed a tenth of everything and gave it to Melchizedek. And this tithe
readings.plain: Abram went and killed Chedorlaomer and came back. He set aside a tenth of everything and gave it to Melchizedek. This tithe

readings.w: Charles's translation (1902; 1913), made from his own Ge'ez text; Charles 1902 marks a gap at the start of the verse
readings.en: (gap) ... for Abram and for his seed

why: The Plain English Translation translates VanderKam's text as printed, brackets included, so the verse reads as a whole; the note on Melchizedek in this verse explains the gap. Without the bracketed words the verse jumps from Abram arming his servants to the middle of a law about tithes. The gap falls exactly where Genesis 14:15–20 tells of the rescue and of Melchizedek.
b: Charles 1902 says plainly that at the start of this verse "there is obviously a lacuna." Whether Jubilees first told of Melchizedek, or a copyist lost the lines, or someone removed them, cannot be known from the manuscripts we have.

p: VanderKam's text says the covenant was made 'on this night'; Charles's translation has 'on that day.'

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
readings.en: and on this night

readings.w: Charles's translation (1902; 1913), made from his own Ge'ez text
readings.en: and on that day

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's text. The night fits the scene: the sun had set (14:17), and in the book's calendar the feast day begins at evening. Charles's "day" matches "On that day" in 14:18 and Genesis 15:18.

t: The fourth week, or the third?
p: The manuscripts read 'fourth' (one has 'seventh'). Charles thought the date should be 'third.'

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); also three of Charles's four manuscripts (a, c, d)
readings.en: of the fourth week

readings.w: Charles's manuscript b (Charles 1902)
readings.en: of the seventh week

readings.w: Charles's correction (1902), following Dillmann, not found in a manuscript
readings.en: of the third week

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the manuscripts' reading. Charles 1902 argued from the book's own dates that the year should fall in the third week, as also in 16:15, and that Dillmann had seen this before him. The book's numbers in these chapters do not always agree with each other.

a: I will give you and your offspring after you the land
p: VanderKam prints the opening words in square brackets; Charles restored them from Genesis 17:8.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989), the words printed in square brackets
readings.orig: ወእሁብ ለከ ወለዘርእከ እምድኅሬከ (wäʾhub läkä wäläzärʾəkä ʾəmdəḫrekä)
readings.en: and I will give to you and to your seed after you
readings.plain: I will give you and your offspring after you the land

readings.w: The manuscripts Charles used, as he reports them (Charles 1902)
readings.en: (words missing)

why: The Plain English Translation includes the bracketed words, as VanderKam's text does. Charles 1902 explains that they were lost when a copyist's eye skipped between two similar endings, and he restored them from Genesis 17:8, which the verse retells. Without them the verse has no verb. The EOTC printed Bible (digital copy) prints the same square brackets here, which shows that it copies VanderKam's text at this point; it is not cited as a witness.

a: Those born in his house, the men of his household
p: VanderKam prints 'those born in his house' in brackets; Charles restored it from the Latin.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989), the words in square brackets; the Latin version (Charles 1902)
readings.en: the son of his house, and the men of his house
readings.plain: Those born in his house, the men of his household

readings.w: The Ge'ez manuscripts Charles used, as he reports them (Charles 1902)
readings.en: and the men of his house

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's text. The Latin, which survives for this part of chapter 15, has the words, and Genesis 17:27 also names "those born in the household." The EOTC printed Bible (digital copy) prints the same square brackets here, which shows that it copies VanderKam's text at this point; it is not cited as a witness.

p: The Ge'ez and the Latin say 'until the eighth day'; Charles changed it to 'on the eighth day.'

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); the Latin version (Charles 1902)
readings.en: until the eighth day

readings.w: Charles's correction (1902), not found in a manuscript
readings.en: on the eighth day

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the text, rendering "until" as "by." Charles 1902 thought "until" gave the wrong sense, since the rite must be done on the eighth day and not before, and blamed a slip in the Hebrew. But "not circumcised by the eighth day" makes good sense: the boy has missed the day.

a: all the angels of the presence and all the angels of holiness
t: Two orders of angels, or more?
p: The Ge'ez names two kinds of angels; the Latin, as Charles reports it, names three or four.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
readings.orig: ኵሎሙ መላእክተ ገጽ ወኵሎሙ መላእክተ ቅዳሴ (kʷəlomu mälaʾkətä gäṣ wäkʷlomu mälaʾkətä qədase)
readings.en: all the angels of the presence and all the angels of holiness
readings.plain: all the angels of the presence and all the angels of holiness

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.orig: angeli vultus ... archangeli benedictionis ... angeli sanctificationis
readings.en: the angels of the face, the archangels of blessing, the angels of sanctification
readings.plain: all the angels of the presence, the archangels of blessing and the angels of holiness

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez. Charles 1902 judged that the Latin "of blessing" had pushed out "of sanctification," so that the passage, like 2:2 and 2:18, speaks of only two highest orders.

a: as we had told Sarah that we would come back to her, and she too had conceived a son
t: A later note in the text?
p: Charles thought these words, with the start of 16:16, a later gloss. Goes with the next variant.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
readings.orig: በከመ ንቤላ ለሳራ ከመ ንግባእ ኀቤሃ ወይእቲሂ ፀንሰት ወልደ (bäkämä nəbela läsara kämä nəgbaʾ ḫäbeha wäyʾətihi ḍänsät wäldä)
readings.en: as we had told Sarah that we would return to her, and she too had conceived a son
readings.plain: as we had told Sarah that we would come back to her, and she too had conceived a son

readings.w: Charles's text (1902), which brackets these words as a gloss
readings.en: (words removed)

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the words, as all the manuscripts do. Charles 1902 judged that they "destroy the sense of the context" and grew out of the hard reading in 16:4. They do repeat 16:4, but they belong to the text as it has come down.

a: We came back in the seventh month and found Sarah pregnant before us.
t: A later note in the text? (continued)
p: Charles bracketed this sentence too, with the end of 16:15.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
readings.orig: ወተመየጥነ በወርኅ ሳብዕ ወረከብናሃ ለሳራ ፅንስተ ቅድሜነ (wätämäyäṭnä bäwärḫ sabʿ wäräkäbnaha läsara ḍənsətä qədmenä)
readings.en: and we returned in the seventh month and found Sarah pregnant before us
readings.plain: We came back in the seventh month and found Sarah pregnant before us.

readings.w: Charles's text (1902), which brackets these words as a gloss
readings.en: (words removed)

why: See the variant on 16:15. All the witnesses have the sentence, and the Plain English Translation keeps it.

a: We blessed her and told her
p: The Ge'ez says the angels blessed Sarah and told her; the Latin says they blessed Abraham and told him.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
readings.en: and we blessed her and told her
readings.plain: We blessed her and told her

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902
readings.en: and we blessed him and told him
readings.plain: We blessed him and told him

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's text. Charles 1902 followed the Latin, because the message that follows is about Abraham ("decreed for him") and because 16:19 says the angels then told Sarah what they had told him. The Latin may well be right, but the Ge'ez can stand: the angels speak to Sarah about her husband.
